chapters.title: Chapter 4: Tax and Rules in India

lessons.title: The Rulebook: SEBI SBEB Regulations and the Companies Act on ESOPs

children.text: Every clause you have read about in this course, the one-year minimum vesting, the exercise price floor, the leaver rules, the trust limits, comes from somewhere. This lesson shows you the two rulebooks those clauses come from, and what each one demands of the company running your scheme.

It matters for three practical reasons. If you are an employee, it tells you what your company cannot legally do to you. If you work in HR, it is your compliance map. If you are a founder, it is the sequence you must follow or your grants are not valid.

body.text: Unlisted companies follow the Companies Act, 2013 and its rules. Listed companies follow those plus the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021. Which rulebook applies to you depends entirely on whether the shares are listed.

children.text: Two Rulebooks, One Subject

columns.label: Unlisted company
points: Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014
Filings with the Registrar of Companies
Wide freedom on exercise price above face value

columns.label: Listed company
points: All of the above, plus the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021
Covers ESOS, ESPS, SARs, general employee benefit and retirement schemes
Shareholder approval, with a separate resolution for a trust route
Continuous disclosure, including in the board’s report
Trust rules, insider trading rules and stock exchange filings on top

children.text: Who Can, and Cannot, Receive Options

Rule 12 defines who counts as an employee for ESOP purposes, and the definition is wider than people expect in one direction and narrower in another. A permanent employee working in India or abroad qualifies, as does a director, whole-time or not, and an employee of a subsidiary, holding or associate company. An
independent director
does not.

markDefs.definition: A non-executive director meeting statutory independence criteria, who is barred from receiving stock options.

cells: Employee of a subsidiary, holding or associate company
Often needs a separate shareholder resolution
Director holding more than 10% of equity
Directly or indirectly, unless the startup exemption applies

body.label: Startup exemption from the promoter and 10% director exclusions
body.context: A DPIIT-recognised startup may grant options to promoters and to directors holding more than 10%, for up to 10 years from incorporation or registration.

body.text: This exemption exists because founder-run startups look nothing like the widely held companies the exclusion was written for. A founder who has diluted to 18% and draws a modest salary is in a very different position from a promoter of a listed group. Note the clock: it runs from incorporation, not from DPIIT recognition.

body.title: Who Cannot Be Granted Options?
body.question: A twelve-year-old unlisted manufacturing company wants to grant options to four people: its CFO, an independent director, a plant manager at its subsidiary, and a co-founder who holds 22% and sits on the board. Who is ineligible?
options: The independent director and the co-founder holding 22%
The independent director and the subsidiary employee
body.explanation: Independent directors are barred outright. A director holding more than 10% is also excluded, and the startup exemption cannot help here because the company is twelve years old and the relief runs for ten years from incorporation. The CFO and the subsidiary plant manager are both eligible, though the subsidiary grant may need a separate shareholder resolution.

children.text: The Sequence a Company Must Follow
Grants are not valid because someone sent an offer letter. They are valid because the company followed the process under
Section 62(1)(b)
and Rule 12.

markDefs.definition: Section 62(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, the provision under which a company issues shares to employees under an ESOP scheme.

body.title: From scheme design to allotted shares

events.title: Draft the scheme
events.description: Set out eligibility, vesting, exercise price or its formula, exercise period, leaver treatment and lapse conditions.

events.title: Board approval
events.description: The board approves the scheme and calls a general meeting.

events.title: Special resolution
events.description: Shareholders approve by special resolution, with an explanatory statement disclosing the prescribed particulars.

events.title: Grant
events.description: The board or a committee grants options to identified employees and issues grant letters.

events.title: Maintain the register
events.description: Details of every grant go into the Register of Employee Stock Options in Form SH-6.

events.title: Allotment and filing
events.description: On exercise, shares are allotted and the return of allotment is filed in Form PAS-3.

body.title: When a second, separate resolution is needed

children.text: A single special resolution approving the scheme is not always enough. A separate shareholder resolution is required for a grant to employees of a subsidiary or holding company, and for a grant to identified employees of one percent or more of the issued capital, excluding outstanding warrants and conversions, in any one year.
Varying the terms of an outstanding scheme also requires a special resolution, and a variation that is detrimental to the interests of employees holding options cannot simply be imposed.
For listed companies, the trust route needs its own separate resolution, on top of the approval for the scheme itself.

body.title: Find the 1% Threshold
body.prompt: A company has an issued capital of 50,00,000 shares. Above what number of options granted to a single identified employee in one year does a separate shareholder resolution become necessary?
body.explanation: One percent of 50,00,000 is 50,000 options. A proposed grant of 60,000 options to one person would cross it and needs its own separate resolution, over and above the resolution approving the scheme.

children.text: Rules That Protect You as an Option Holder
Options cannot be transferred.
You cannot sell, gift, pledge, hypothecate or mortgage your options, and nobody other than you can exercise them. They are personal to you.
No shareholder rights before exercise.
An option carries no dividend and no vote. Those arrive only when you exercise and become a shareholder.
At least one year before vesting.
The minimum gap between grant and vesting, relaxed only on death or permanent incapacity.
Terms cannot be quietly worsened.
Varying an outstanding scheme requires a special resolution, and variations detrimental to existing option holders need their interests to be respected.
The company must keep records.
Form SH-6 and the board’s report disclosures mean there is an auditable trail of what you were granted.

body.text: Because options cannot be pledged or transferred, they cannot be used as collateral for a loan to fund your own exercise. Employees planning a large exercise sometimes discover this late. Your options are not an asset a bank will lend against.

body.title: The Approval Bar
body.textWithBlank: An ESOP scheme must be approved by shareholders through a ___ resolution, which needs at least three fourths of the votes cast in favour.
body.explanation: An ordinary resolution, carried by simple majority, is not sufficient. The higher bar reflects that an ESOP scheme dilutes every existing shareholder.

children.text: What HR and Founders Must Keep Straight

body.title: The Compliance Trail for an Indian ESOP Scheme
steps: Scheme document approved by the board and by a shareholder special resolution
Explanatory statement covering the prescribed particulars, including vesting, exercise price and lapse conditions
Separate resolutions where required, for subsidiary or holding company employees, for grants of 1% or more, and for a trust route at a listed company
Grant letters issued to identified employees, with dates and quantities recorded
Register of Employee Stock Options maintained in Form SH-6
Form PAS-3 filed with the Registrar of Companies on each allotment
Disclosures made in the board’s report, and for listed companies the additional SEBI and exchange filings
Perquisite valuation and TDS handled correctly at each exercise

body.title: The Founder Who Wants a Grant
body.scenario: Sanjana incorporated her analytics company six years ago and is DPIIT recognised. After three funding rounds she holds 19% and is a whole-time director. She has taken a below-market salary throughout and wants the board to grant her 40,000 options. The company has 50,00,000 issued shares. Her CFO says promoters cannot receive ESOPs.
body.prompt: Is the CFO right, and what does the company need to do?
body.modelAnswer: The CFO is stating the general rule but missing the exception. Promoters and directors holding more than 10% are ordinarily excluded, but a DPIIT-recognised startup is exempt from both exclusions for ten years from incorporation, and the company is six years old, so a grant to Sanjana is permissible for about four more years. The company must still follow the full process: a scheme covering the grant, board approval, and a shareholder special resolution with a proper explanatory statement. At 40,000 options against 50,00,000 issued shares she is at 0.8%, below the one percent threshold that would force a separate resolution, though that is worth rechecking if the grant is increased or if she receives more in the same year. Two further points matter: the ten-year clock runs from incorporation rather than from DPIIT recognition, so the window is narrower than founders often assume, and investors will scrutinise a founder grant closely, so the commercial case for it should be documented alongside the legal one.

children.text: A Moving Target

This is an area where the rules genuinely change. The SBEB regulations themselves were consolidated in 2021, bringing ESOS, ESPS, SARs, general employee benefit schemes, retirement benefit schemes and sweat equity under a single framework. There has since been active discussion at SEBI about the treatment of options held by founders who become classified as promoters ahead of an IPO, an issue that has caught several Indian startups on their way to listing. If that applies to you, take current professional advice rather than relying on any general summary.

cards.definition: The Companies Act provision under which shares are issued to employees under an ESOP scheme.
The rule setting out eligibility, the one-year vesting minimum, disclosures and leaver treatment.
Shareholder approval needing three fourths of votes cast. Required for any ESOP scheme.
The statutory Register of Employee Stock Options a company must maintain.
The return of allotment filed with the Registrar when shares are allotted on exercise.
SEBI’s consolidated framework for share-based employee benefits at listed companies.

points: Unlisted companies follow the Companies Act and Rule 12. Listed companies follow those plus the SEBI SBEB and Sweat Equity Regulations, 2021.
Permanent employees, including those posted abroad, and most directors are eligible. Independent directors are not.
Promoters and directors holding over 10% are excluded, but DPIIT-recognised startups are exempt for 10 years from incorporation.
Every scheme needs a shareholder special resolution, with separate resolutions for subsidiary grants, grants of 1% or more, and the listed company trust route.
Options cannot be transferred or pledged, so they cannot be used as loan collateral.
An option gives no dividend and no vote until you exercise it.
Companies must keep a Form SH-6 register and file Form PAS-3 on allotment, which gives you an auditable record of your grants.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal advice. It summarises a framework that runs to many pages and changes periodically, and it omits procedural detail that matters in practice. Companies designing or amending a scheme should work with a company secretary or counsel.
